sections.html:
For 2026, a Sugar Land property owner pays the city $0.371116 for every $100 of taxable value. That is just the city slice. Your school district, Fort Bend County and any MUD or LID district bill separately and stack on top.

Inside that figure, $0.220157 pays for day-to-day operations and $0.150959 goes to debt service, the money that repays what the city borrowed for projects.

The city portion is roughly 21 percent of the residential bill in Fort Bend ISD and 19 percent in Lamar CISD, before any MUD or LID taxes. Check your bill to see which district serves your house.

The city rate edged up in both Tax Year 2025 and Tax Year 2026.

City of Sugar Land tax rate per $100 of taxable value
ComponentTY2026TY2025TY2024
Maintenance and operations$0.220157$0.207172$0.207172
Debt service$0.150959$0.151655$0.146038
Total$0.371116$0.358827$0.353210

Two 2026 benchmarks: a no-new-revenue rate of $0.355381 and a voter-approval rate of $0.381586, the ceiling that needs a vote to exceed. On the median homestead, the city portion of the bill is estimated at $1,371 for 2026, up from $1,312 a year earlier.

The council votes each September, once the budget is approved and a hearing has been held. The deadline is 60 days after the certified roll arrives, or September 30 if that is later. Appraised values are certified by July 25, so the rate cannot be final until that roll is in.

Two benchmark rates guide the vote. One, the no-new-revenue rate, would collect the prior year's dollars from existing property. The other, the voter-approval rate, caps what council can adopt without an election: debt service plus 3.5 percent more in operating revenue.

The city's taxpayer impact statement shows a $4.90 monthly impact for the median homestead in 2026.

Sugar Land calls its rate one of the lowest in Texas for a city this size. It has dropped from 50 cents in 1993 to 35 cents per $100, which the city credits to economic development and sales tax growth, while the city homestead exemption climbed from 1 percent to 15 percent.

The city average home value is $540,358 for 2026, compared with $529,032 for 2025, and the average homestead exemption is $81,054. Treat those as averages only. Price your house from your own notice and bill.

The city homestead exemption equals 15 percent of assessed value. Owners over 65 and disabled persons get a flat $70,000 as well, though an owner who is both receives only one. A disabled veteran should call the appraisal district about a separate exemption.

School districts set exemptions separately. The state school homestead amount is $140,000, and seniors and disabled owners get $60,000 more plus a ceiling that generally freezes their school bill at the first qualifying year's level.

  • Own it, live in it as your main home, and claim no second homestead anywhere.
  • If the seller never claimed one, a buyer closing after New Year's Day can claim for the rest of that year.
  • Applications go to the appraisal district, not to the city.

Two county offices touch your bill. Fort Bend Central Appraisal District decides what the house is worth. Fort Bend County's Tax Assessor-Collector mails statements and takes payment for the city. Value and exemption disputes start with the first.

The appraisal district is at 2801 B F Terry Blvd, Rosenberg, TX 77471, phone 281-344-8623. Exemption applications need a copy of your Texas driver's license or DPS ID, and the address on it must match the property address.

If you recently bought, bring your closing statement or deed, since the office may ask who owned the home on that date. Texas appraises property as of January 1. Notices for single-family homesteads go out around April 1, protests are generally due mid-May and the appraisal records are approved in July. A value you want to dispute has to be challenged inside that window.

Your window closes January 31. Anything still unpaid in February is delinquent. When the bill is mailed after January 10, the cutoff slides to the first of a later month that leaves 21 days or more. Seniors and disabled owners can spread payment over four installments.

  • On February 1 a bill picks up a 6 percent penalty and 1 percent interest.
  • Each month adds more penalty until it tops out at 12 percent on July 1.
  • Interest keeps running with no ceiling, and a collection lawyer's fee of up to 20 percent may follow.

Pay before the first of any month and you avoid the next step up in penalty. For a house you are about to sell, that is one more reason to clear the balance early rather than let closing absorb it.

Closing the sale leaves that year's bill in place. From January 1 the lien clings to the land, and the person who held title that morning stays answerable for the tax.

So the closing agent orders a tax certificate and settles any balance with money from the seller's side. An unpaid account moves through notices, an optional installment plan and finally a suit, with costs added. A taxing unit can ultimately foreclose and auction the house.

If back taxes are why you want to sell, call the Fort Bend County Tax Assessor-Collector for a payoff number before you price the house. With that figure you can compare an agent listing, a private deal and a cash offer fairly. Penalty and interest can sometimes be waived when the tax is paid soon after you learn of the delinquency, so raise that with the tax office. A cash sale skips lender approval, but the tax still gets paid at closing. Ask the title company to list every payoff it expects, such as tax, any mortgage and any lien, so you can see your net before you accept an offer.

sections.h2: Protesting your value before a sale
sections.html:
Thinking of listing in spring? Read the appraisal notice first. A lower value shrinks the tax proration at closing and shows buyers the bill is manageable. Homestead notices go out near April 1, protests are generally due mid-May, and the records are approved in July.

Take the notice, the deed and evidence for your number, such as recent sales nearby or repair estimates. Questions about a protest go to the Fort Bend Central Appraisal District, not the city or the tax office.

Any buyer, cash or financed, will ask about the current value and your last bill, so have both ready. It speeds up price talks and shows you know the property.

faqs.q: What is the 2026 city tax rate in Sugar Land?
faqs.a: $0.371116 per $100 of taxable value. School, county and any MUD or LID rates come on top.

faqs.q: Does Sugar Land give a homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Yes, 15 percent of assessed value, with an extra $70,000 for owners over 65 or for disabled persons, one or the other. Apply through the appraisal district.

faqs.q: Who gets my Sugar Land tax payment?
faqs.a: The county Tax Assessor-Collector takes it on the city's behalf. Questions about value or exemptions belong with the appraisal district.

faqs.q: When does a Sugar Land bill go delinquent?
faqs.a: The day after January 31. A 6 percent penalty and 1 percent interest are added starting February 1.

faqs.q: Can I sell if I owe taxes on my Sugar Land house?
faqs.a: Yes, the balance comes out of your sale proceeds at the closing table. Request a payoff amount from the county tax office ahead of time.
